name: Photofeeler testing

lead: Photofeeler is a website where anonymous voters rate your photo, giving you numerical scores and comments on how strangers perceive you. Looksmaxxing forums use the scores as an informal gauge of looks and of which photo to post.

In dating tests, voters score attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness; business and social tests use other traits. The company has published its own analyses and a 2019 paper by its staff on a neural network trained on its data.

paras: Users upload a photo into a business, social or dating test, receive scores and anonymous comments, and swap in new photos to compare. Voters earn credits by rating other people's photos.
Low physical risk. Forum members report scores that feel discouraging or biased toward smiles, and some report results that did not match dating-app performance. Photos are shown to strangers.

angle.text: Uploading a photo shows how anonymous voters score attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness, which guides which pictures you use. Members disagree on how well the scores track real-world results, and the company's own analyses are the published evidence.

lead: Photofeeler testing is the practice of uploading a photograph to Photofeeler, a website where anonymous voters rate it, in order to see how strangers perceive the person pictured. Photofeeler was founded in 2013 in Boulder, Colorado, by Ben Peterson and Ann Pierce, and offers business, social and dating test types.[1]

In dating tests, voters score a photo on attractiveness, trustworthiness and smartness; the other test types use different traits. Users receive numerical scores and anonymous comments, and voters earn or buy credits by rating other people's photos.[1] Looksmaxxing forums use the site as an informal gauge of facial attractiveness and of which photo to use, and members disagree about how well its scores track real-world results.

Published evidence specific to the site consists of the company's own analyses and a 2019 paper by Photofeeler staff describing a neural network trained on its data; no independent clinical studies of Photofeeler testing as a looksmaxxing method were found.[1]
infobox: Credits bought or earned by voting[1]

paras: A user uploads a photo, chooses a test category and receives votes from other users. According to Wikipedia, business tests score competence, likability and influence, social tests score confidence, authenticity and fun, and dating tests score smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness.[1] Grokipedia describes scores as percentile-style figures from 1 to 10 standardised against people of the same gender and age and adjusted for individual voter tendencies, with confidence intervals that narrow as votes accumulate.
Voters pay for results by rating other people's photos, which earns credits, or by purchasing credits. The site says it uses fraud filters and AI processing to discard invalid votes.[1]

A 2014 analysis of more than 60,000 ratings of 800 business photos reported that a smile showing teeth gave the largest boost to likability and that formal attire raised perceived competence and influence.[1] In 2019 Agastya Kalra and Ben Peterson published Photofeeler-D3, a neural network trained on 1.2 million dating photos, which the paper reported predicted perceived smartness, trustworthiness and attractiveness about as well as roughly ten averaged human votes.[1] These are company-authored findings.

Members of looksmax.org post their Photofeeler scores as a rough numerical rating of their looks, compare results, and discuss how to read them. Some filter by voter gender and age; one poster noted that the site had begun allowing a female-only voter setting without payment.

Opinions diverge. One poster reported that his highest-rated photo performed poorly on Tinder while his lowest-rated photo performed well, and said the voters appeared biased toward smiling photos. Another member argued that needing the site to judge one's looks implies the person is not attractive, which a reply disputed. A separate thread title asks whether a smile or no-smile photo scores better.
No studies found. The only research identified is the company's own analyses and a neural-network paper by its staff, described above.[1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, Photofeeler scores serve as an informal looks metric and a way to compare photos, with recurring debate about bias and real-world relevance.

claims.claim: Photofeeler scores are a fair measure of how attractive you are
High Photofeeler scores do not translate into dating-app success
Voters are biased toward smiling photos

timeline.event: Company analysis of 60,000+ ratings of business photos reported on smiles and attire.[1]
Photofeeler-D3 neural network paper published by Kalra and Peterson.[1]
